utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Everyone, welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-99-36-T, The Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you. Can you follow in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And good morning to you. Appearances, Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours, Ms. Sureta Chana, Julian Nicholls, assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Appearances for the Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: David Cunningham and Aleksandar Vujic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good morning to you, too. Any preliminaries before we proceed? No?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: We do have the English version of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The 608?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Perhaps that can be distributed later. In the meantime, let's bring in the witness, please. I take it that today -- how long do you anticipate --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I will be finished before the first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which basically means that we adjourn?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: It means we have no objection to adjourning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, it-- we reserve all opposition, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman is preparing for the next witness who we're going to proof this afternoon and we'll be ready to go in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The next witness will be here for how long do you expect?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Two days maximum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I think it might be comparable to this witness in terms of his direct examination. I think it might be a bit longer because he comes from Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And who is going to cross-examine him?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm not sure, Your Honour, at this point. Probably Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So yes, usher, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this is 2608 if I remember the number well. No?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Savic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome again once more. You don't need to repeat the solemn declaration. I just want to remind you that you are testifying under an oath, the solemn declaration that you made -- you entered yesterday. So take a seat, and let's get started so that you leave this place the earlier -- the sooner the better. Yes, Madam Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Today I want to ask you some questions about the paramilitary formations. Yesterday, you told this Court -- the transcript, Your Honours, is at page 25. And this was when you were shown the document P400. And that is the Main Staff report about the problems the paramilitaries were causing in the Prnjavor Municipality.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Prnjavor, yes. Thank you for that. And you said that Veljko Milankovic, they caused problems. I'm reading from the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: They caused problems, not only in Prnjavor, but also in the general region of Prnjavor. And that resulted in some problems. And you went on to say: I wanted him disarmed and placed under the command of the Yugoslav People's Army. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: If you look -- if I can show the witness P400 again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I've got a copy of P400 right here in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I want to take you to page 2 of that report. And it starts off with "Many formations of this type..." Have you found that particular line, Mr. Savic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 2?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, page 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, could...

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Perhaps it's on the first page of the B/C/S. It's this one. Yes, it's just that English typing is larger than the B/C/S, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: It would be the fourth point where it talks about the characteristics of the paramilitary group. Have you got -- it's the fourth point.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise, Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Have you found the place, Mr. Savic? "Many formations of this type..."

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's on page 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Now, if I can read it to you, the Main Staff report says that: "Many formations of this type displayed hatred of the non-Serbian peoples and one can conclude without reservation that they are the genocidal element among the Serbian people."

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I'm reading here.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Savic, did you think it was a good idea to have these genocidal elements included into the army?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question. Is it a good idea to do what?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Because you had said in your transcript yesterday that you wanted these paramilitary formations disbanded or put under the control of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, Veljko Milankovic, who was the commander of the Wolves of Vucak, that's right, is it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I thought you were making a comment. But he was the commander of that paramilitary group in Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And he was involved in the takeover of the Kozara mountain in August 1992, the transmitter. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I had that information.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And as of 5th June, I know you were not there at the time, were you aware that he was put under the command of the 1KK?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see that document, but I did have some information to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Well, I'll show you P1802, P1802.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I have the B/C/S if I can assist the usher.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: This is from the command of the 1st Krajina Corps signed by General Talic, is it not? And if you look at point 2 --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: -- Would you agree -- you would now agree that he was appointed the commander of the 327th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says in the document. He was appointed as battalion commander of the 327th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I would now like to show you P1803 and ask you: Were you aware that he was actually given a decoration, a posthumous decoration for his service to the army?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had that information.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And this document at point 5 reflects that, does it not?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I would like to show the witness, it's not a tendered document, ERN 03081715 to 1732. It's from Glas, Your Honours. Open sources. Yes, this can be given P2707, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Have you ever seen this before?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't. I'm reading this for the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Chana, if you're going to ask him questions based on any part of this, then we need to give him time to read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, he can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Savic, take your time, please. Go through the article. If he has never seen it before, I think he needs to read it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't read too well without my glasses, but I think I have got the gist of the article. So you may proceed asking me questions, Madam Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: This is an interview of Mr. Milankovic, is it not? It's reporting on an interview? Can I point you to the -- I don't know what page it would be for you, where he says, and I quote: "We were the victims of a political game."

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And then the next paragraph, and I'll read that out, says: "Although it's not time for disputes among the Serbs, I must say something. We were a unit of the Autonomous Region of the Bosnian Krajina. The president of the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of the Bosnian Krajina, Vojo Kupresanin, and the Prime Minister, Andjelko Grahovac, as well as the members of that government, and the leadership of the Banja Luka SDS were fully informed about all our operations. Actually, we took part in operations at the order of the leadership of the Autonomous Region of Bosnian Krajina." Would you agree that that was the case? Would you agree with the sentiments expressed by Milankovic when he says this?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Knowing Milankovic as a criminal before the war, I wouldn't believe his words because he was a liar, to put it that way. Who was his commander, how things were arranged, it is very hard to say. He was pretty much his own agent. He organised plundering. His unit consisted of well-known criminals. So I would not be able to confirm this statement of his. He used to brag a lot also.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: From your own knowledge of the events in the region, would you say that there's any truth in this?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning, there is some truth, but let me point you to the first passage. The MUP units of BH disarmed him. They were on paper members of the MUP, but Delimustafic never sent any forces to capture him. Those forces were organised from Prnjavor and Banja Luka. At the beginning when it says walk on Serbian thorns, it's a lie, a notorious lie. So this statement is nothing but him bragging about being subordinated to somebody. Very often, he would issue false statements for the press. So when you look at the first passage from the first word to the last, it's all lies.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, he was court-martialed, he was tried in a court-martial court, was he not? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about that. There was no court-martial. It didn't exist. He was tried several times before the war. And during the war, several criminal reports were filed against him.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now in the last -- I don't know what page it is, it's 6 in the English page. "From the ruling of the military court in Banja Luka." This is where the ruling says that Milankovic would not be criminally prosecuted for the above-mentioned crimes because there were no justified grounds to suspect the accused Milankovic committed these or other crimes for which he is charged ex officio.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: This is from the investigating judge, Lieutenant-Colonel Vujanovic [phoen]? So he was released, was he not? And continued --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: -- combat operations? Do you know, are you aware that he that his unit --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the war started in 1992. He continued with combat operations, and his unit grew into a bigger unit of the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, when you arrested him, you found a large number of weapons and other items, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What happened to them? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the weapons?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, the weapons that you found --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did find weapons, all sorts of weapons, small arms mostly, and we packed all of that and transported it to Banja Luka and handed it over to the corps in the military post in Banja Luka. So all the weapons were handed over to the military in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: But they disappeared, did they not?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. It was with the army. What happened with the weapons later on, I really don't know. I wouldn't be able to tell you. All I can tell you that we handed the weapons over to the military in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: On the last page of this particular document.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me try and find it here.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: The title is "Where are the Weapons?"

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: It was reported, was it not, and I quote: "When Veljko Milankovic and his fighters were arrested, 20 pistols, 50 Zoljas, hand-held rocket launchers, and a variety of other weapons were seized. But a certificate on the confiscation of the weapons was not issued to them. When the military court ruled that all the confiscated items were to be returned to them, the weapons were missing. Where are the weapons? Is a question" -- I'm sorry, I'm speaking too fast. I apologise to the translators. "When the confiscated items were returned to them, the weapons were missing. Where the weapons are is a question which Milenko Savic, the chief of the public security station in Prnjavor at the time and military security forces which participated in this operation should answer. Milankovic said he knew for sure that the Zoljas remained in the Prnjavor public security station, but they have simply vanished into thin air." They were never recovered, were they?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not true. This is not true. As usually he told lies. This is just one of his stories to divert attention to myself, to blacken me with the people and the leadership in Prnjavor. And I claim with full responsibility that all the weapons were handed over in Banja Luka, and there are documents testifying to that. I'm sure that you will still be able to locate it in the public security station in Prnjavor and in Banja Luka. We were very careful about all this because they -- we were aware of the fact that he had said that Alija Delimustafic came from Sarajevo with his Green Berets to disarm them, whereas it was us from Prnjavor and Banja Luka. I'm sorry that I don't have the time to read the whole article, but I'm sure that 95 per cent of it is blatant lies. So when I'm reading this subtitle "Where are the Weapons?", all of this is a lie. And Milankovic was known to brag a lot. He would always give himself higher ranks. He would always engage in name-dropping, mentioning some leaders in the area, but that would simply be bragging and not true.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Right. Now, let me go to the Mice in Teslic where you also participated in that arrest, is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: You -- do you know who brought the Mice into Teslic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are several versions of that story. Some say that it was the official municipal authorities. Some say that they came from another centre of power. But the fact is that they did arrive in Teslic. I wouldn't be able to tell you exactly who brought them and who asked for their arrival in Teslic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: One minute, Your Honour. I'm looking for P1939. Can the usher please assist me with P1939.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: It's a document dated 17th August 1992, and it's signed by the chief of the centre. At the beginning of that document, it talks about the arrest of a group of persons in Teslic on 30th June 1992. That would be the Mice, would it not?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And it says: "At the request of Nikola Perisic, president of the Teslic Municipal Assembly, and following a written authorisation, operative commander Colonel Simic, First-Class Ljubisa Petricevic selected a group of uniformed members of the military police," and it gives names. Do you recognise any of these names?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some names I do recognise, Vitomir Devic and so on and so forth. I am familiar with some of these names.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: But they do belong to the Mice, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And it says that "in addition to the said group, at the request of President Perisic, another group of ten uniformed persons were sent to Teslic, Doboj CSB security services."

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And it talks about, over the page, that a lot of ammunition and artillery was also seized at the time of the arrest. And it says that "during the arrest, the following items were seized from these individuals without due issuance of receipts." These weapons also disappeared, did they not, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't. These weapons were also handed over. And most of these weapons did not disappear. Those people who had sent this group to do what they did in Teslic sought justification for their acts, and this is nothing else but that. Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 22473 to 22476.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I would like to show the witness P1947, please. 1947. I have the B/C/S. Would you like to take mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: This document is a crime situation in the area of the Teslic Municipality from June to September 1992. And it's by the public Prosecutor, Branko Peric.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Branko Peric.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Branko Peric. Yes, sorry about my pronunciation. And I want you to go to the second page where it says "the actual crime situation...", please. Now, this is after the Mice had been arrested, is it not, the date of this document? And it's talking about the crime situation in Teslic after the Mice had been arrested?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And gotten rid of?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And it says that "the recorded crime is a fraction of the real crime existing in society today. Most criminal acts remain undiscovered, and many crimes are tolerated by the authorities for various reasons. The Prosecutor's Office has knowledge of the day-to-day looting of property, houses, and business premises being set on fire and destroyed, armed robbery and murder being committed for base motives, socially owned flats and private houses being occupied unlawfully, the stealing of forest timbers. There is no criminal prosecution for most of these acts." So would it not be true, then, to say that the crime continued and went unpunished in the Teslic Municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may be said so, if you don't take into account the period before the 2nd of June. These figures were even worse during the period between the 31st of May and the 2nd of June. What is your ground for comparison? If you have that document, you will see that measures were taken and that curfew was introduced and people could only walk freely around the town for three hours. It all depends on what your grounds of comparison are. It is true that there was crime, but there were no murders, there were no killings, no -- except for the killings in the army. And if you look at this period and compare it with the period between March and June, the three-month period between March and June, then this report would be much better, much more favourable in comparison with that period. It all depends on what this period is compared with. So basically if -- I'm not saying that there was no crime. There was looting. There was plunder. There were thefts. We had huge problems. There were armed attacks against the police. There were renegade soldiers, renegade police officers who did not want to put themselves under the control of either the army or the police. So it was bad, but it was not as drastic as one would think when you look at this document. And I remember that people when they stopped me in the street, that they would cry because they were so thankful to me. I know Branko Peric personally. He is a very conscientious prosecutor. He processed quite a lot of crimes at that time, which was a courageous act at that time. I'm not denying that there were crimes, but these figures are much better than the figures that you would find in the period between the 31st of March and the 1st of June of that same year.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Savic. The Mice were also released. They were not prosecuted?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And they continued combat operations, right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what they did after that. But they did not come back to the area of Teslic while we were there as part of the Banja Luka security centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: That's all I have from this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Chana. Mr. Cunningham, I understand, has no redirect?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I have no redirect. I just would like to wish the witness a safe trip home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have any questions, Judge Janu? Yes, Mr. Savic, Judge Taya from Japan has some questions for you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Do you know the fate of those 1.350 people, at least 1.000 people, after being freed from jail in Teslic? They were not detained once again after being freed by Milankovic's soldiers or by whoever.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I reply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Veljko Milankovic was not active on that territory. That is a misunderstanding. As for the fate of that 1.300 people, I don't know the exact number, they all went home and they were grateful to us. I knew some of those people. Some of them are still in Teslic, while some left later on to go to another country. However, most of them did come back afterwards. After the collection centres were dissolved, they went to their homes and they were not arrested again. There may have been isolated incidents, but they were quite safe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: During your working in SJB Banja Luka from April to the end of 1992, who were in the position to give you orders? Can you give names of all those people.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. My immediate superior was Slobodan Djurdjevic. He was the chief of my department when I returned to Banja Luka from Teslic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Orders were given orally always, without any justifiable supporting papers?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, the orders I received were oral, and certain financial documents were shown to me, which I was supposed to control or check on in companies whether state-owned or private. So it was usual in my department for orders to be given orally, and the same situation still obtains in the MUP, unless something was exceptional or highly confidential or high risk. And in that case, written plans were drawn up and written orders issued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Were you in the position to know with the organisation from which those orders first originated?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I have known?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Yes, were you in the position to know?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course the chief of the centre who was at the head of the pyramid had all the information, and he could issue orders through Slobodan Djurdjevic, and we mostly operated at the request of aggrieved parties and pursuant to information received from the terrain, from the ground. Perhaps a car was stolen or something was stolen, so this information arrived from different levels and different places. If we received information that in a company somebody had appropriated a hundred thousand euros, for example, we would first check the information, and then our chief would issue us with an oral order to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: As far as you know, those orders have never originated from firstly the ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, no they did not directly come to the department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Nor indirectly, but they firstly originated from?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible, but the police was quite independent because it had its usual scheme of work. And these orders which arrived could arrive from higher levels, but they did not in our case, in the centre of public security. There were 10 or 20 people there, and now I think about it, no, no, we didn't receive orders from higher up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Judge Taya. I have got one simple question for you, Mr. Savic: Would you agree looking back at the event of Mr. Milankovic's arrest and subsequent release that he enjoyed some kind of protection from higher up?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would agree, yes, he did enjoy certain protection. But I also have to say that Veljko was a very dangerous criminal before the war, and people were afraid of him regardless of the post they held. He had 23 serious crimes, or rather criminal reports behind him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you know if in actual fact he received a decoration posthumously after he died? Are you aware whether he received --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. There are documents to that effect, and I did have that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the military chain of command was, but the document was drawn up by the person who decorated him. Whether it was a military or a civilian decoration, I don't know. But -- well, he was decorated. I was not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. I don't have any further questions for you. Judge Janu now has a question for you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Mr. Savic, it's obvious that you tried to do your work decently and faithfully as a good policeman, and you could see that nobody appreciated that at that time. You could see that others were decorated. What was your explanation at that time? How did you -- you are an intelligent, educated man. You -- I believe there was some explanation.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have an explanation, and I still don't to this day. This is the first time I have seen this text. I didn't follow the press. But I always hoped that the war would be over one day. And I think, and I'm deeply convinced, that things will fall into place. Well, I'm glad I wasn't decorated, in view of everything I did and went through, perhaps I deserved it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Was it apparent at that time that everybody who didn't behave simply, say, your way, who didn't stick to the law was part of something what wasn't proper? Was this apparent to everybody at that time generally, that there is going on something what is not at all fair?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, many ordinary people thought the way I did. And they were opposed to everything that was happening so that ordinary people just like me hoped that better times lay ahead. And in Prnjavor, most people still praise my actions, both Serbs and non-Serbs. However, that was what the times were like. We were divided between those who wanted war and those who didn't want war. And I most of the populations didn't want war, but it was imposed on us. That is a broad topic, perhaps, and not something I can go into in this courtroom. But individuals came to the fore who did not deserve to be praised or written about in newspapers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: So everybody was able to make his or her choice where to belong? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for the most part, but it was dangerous. It was dangerous not to behave the way people around you were behaving, but everybody had that option. The choice carried a certain risk with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Janu, and thank you, Judge Taya. Thank you, Mr. Savic. That brings us to the end of your testimony which basically means you're free to go back home. You will be escorted out of the courtroom by Madam usher, and you will be attended and receive all the assistance that you require to enable you to return home. On my behalf, on behalf of the Trial Chamber, on behalf of the parties here, Madam Chana for the Prosecution and Mr. Cunningham for the Defence, I wish to thank you for having come over to give testimony. And on behalf of everyone, I also wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good-bye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So yes, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: It's just a housekeeping matter, it's my understanding that the Glas article dealing with Milankovic is P2707.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's how I have marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I just wanted to make sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just this, Your Honour, I just want to make sure that, well, I just want to get if we can a firm list of witnesses after we take this next break and come back November 26th up until the Christmas break. I know there has been some shifting around because of witnesses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I imagine there will be more shifting when Mr. Ackerman and Mr. Cunningham come back from wherever they are going.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But can we get any confirmation as of today that the list is staying as we received it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Can I call and just let you know because I know that Mr. Ackerman is working on that this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It does create problems --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have every reason to believe that this matter will be looked into by Mr. Ackerman, and we'll have pretty much a clear idea of what to expect and who.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And the last question -- sorry. The last question, is there any additional witness statement for the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So we are going to adjourn until tomorrow morning at 9.00. And your witness has arrived, I take it, Mr. Cunningham?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: My understanding is he comes in around noon today because we're proofing at 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If there is a problem or anything, please do let us know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Any further business? No, okay. We stand adjourned until tomorrow morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To be reconvened on Wednesday, the 12th day of November, 2003, at 9.00 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 10.04 a.m.
